requested.title: IPv6 translation prefixes can disguise private IPv4 destinations

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: The current `isPrivateAddress` rejects the stated `64:ff9b:1::a9fe:a9fe` example because its NAT64 branch matches every address beginning `64:ff9b`, including the local-use prefix; that portion of the finding is inaccurate. However, `::ffff:0:169.254.169.254` is normalized as IPv6 and expands to `[0,0,0,0,0xffff,0,0xa9fe,0xa9fe]`. It bypasses the mapped/compatible IPv4 check because that check requires `g4 === 0`, then returns `false` without evaluating the embedded private IPv4 address. Consequently `assertPublicHttpUrl` accepts an HTTP URL such as `http://[::ffff:0:a9fe:a9fe]/`, and `safeFetch` passes that literal address to `pinnedRequest`; pinning prevents DNS rebinding but does not make an incorrectly accepted destination safe. An authenticated project owner can persist such a value as an integration webhook, after which issue events cause server-side POSTs to it; authenticated link-preview/favicon flows provide other user-controlled `safeFetch` entry points. Authentication, owner checks, CSRF protections, redirect validation, and response-size caps do not protect against a malicious authorized user choosing an internal destination. In a deployment with an IPv4-translated IPv6/SIIT route, this address can be translated to the IPv4 link-local metadata endpoint, creating a concrete SSRF path. Git history shows this relevant logic remains unchanged from the original safe-fetch implementation, and tests cover only the well-known NAT64 prefix and ordinary mapped/compatible forms, not `::ffff:0:0/96`.
